per_ply.human_comment:
Hasting. August,5 - September,2 1895. A prestigious tournament,
organized in order to compare the playing strength of the top chess champions
at that time. Chigorin, Lasker, Tarrasch, Steinitz, Schlechter and other 17
players were participating. All of them were very strong players. Among them
Janowsky and a new talented american player Harry Nelson Pillsbury, who won
the tournament with 16.5 points out of 21. Janowsky, for various reasons not
at his best playing strength, was however successfull in defending his
reputation he had gained in Paris.
per_ply.system_comment: The game opens as a King's Pawn Game (B00).
The game transposes into the King's Knight Opening (C40).
The game transposes into the Ruy Lopez (C60).

per_ply.human_comment:
Steinitz, always faithful to his favoured defense, this time has
improved it with the move a7-a6.
per_ply.system_comment: This is the last book move of the Spanish: Modern Steinitz, 5.O-O Ne7 (C72); both sides are on their own from here.

Na5 is the most accurate move, holding the balance at (+0.12, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Na5 d4 Nxb3 axb3 Ng6], as Black immediately targets the bishop on b3—pressure that can force awkward recaptures or tie White down. Ng6 also leads to equality along [pv:Ng6 a3 Be7 d3 O-O], a roughly comparable alternative, though Na5 is preferred for maintaining that direct challenge to the b3 bishop.

per_ply.human_comment:
What is that? Some strange impulse or a new idea? Janowsky seems ready
to give his lightsquare Bishop for the sake of attack. Is that too much?
Pillsbury, categorically, commented: "Such a move should cost the game to
White."

per_ply.system_comment: The most accurate move, holding the balance at (+0.11, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nf5 Bxf5 exf5 c4 Ba4+], immediately targets the knight on e7 and may cost Black the bishop-pair edge that often dominates on open boards as the line unfolds. Qh5 was a comparable option that leads to equality along [pv:Qh5 g6 Qf3 Nxb3 Nxb3], where White could eventually hold a knight for a bishop.

per_ply.human_comment:
(?) Pillsbury again: "Probably this
exchange is a real mistake. A deadly mistake, I would say. After 9...Bxf5 10.
exf5 White would have lost a piece without compensation." Is it possible that
both Janowsky and Steinitz overlooked the simple continuation suggested by
Pillsbury? Uhmm ... hard to believe.  And in fact, the moves 9... Bxf5 10.
exf5 c4 11. Nc3 (!)  cxb3 12. axb3  followed  by Rf1-e1 and Nc3-d5 (or Nc3-e4)
should make worry the Black's conductor. Let's say that his position, with the
King in the middle of the chessboard, half-undressed, seems at least unclear.
Open windows and doors create air currents which are dangerous for healt. If,
for instance, 12...Nxf5 then 13.Qd5 would win the piece back with advantage.
If then White would play at once 11.Re1, Black, before taking the Bishop,
should scratch his head and think about it one, two, ten times before doing it.
Maybe Pillsbury, with the presumption tha can be told from his words, did "pee
counter wind", to use an italian expression.
Of course now it is too late to play 10...c4 because of 11.Qe2+.

Maybe Steinitz has been too quick in willing to eliminate
the dangerous lightsquare Bishop. Maybe, probably, surely indeed, Janowsky
will show us that his opponent "fell out the frying pan into the fire"!
per_ply.system_comment: The best move, Re1+, holds the balance at (+0.08, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Re1+ Be7 f6 gxf6 axb3], pinning a black piece—a pin can tie down the defender until the pressure is resolved. In return, Black has a bishop and a pawn for a knight. The comparable axb3 also leads to equality via [pv:axb3 Bxf5 Re1+ Be6 Nc3], opening the a-file for White's rook while White keeps a knight for a bishop, yet Re1+ keeps sharper pressure with the pin. The line may steer toward f6 and exchanges that could leave Black with doubled, isolated pawns.

11...Be7 is the most accurate move, holding the balance at (+0.11, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Be7 f6 gxf6 axb3 Be6], steering toward...f6 and exchanges that may later leave Black with doubled, isolated pawns to manage. The runner-up 11...Kd7 is clearly weaker, leading to a clear advantage for White along [pv:Kd7 axb3 Kc7 Bf4 g5], where Black may target the bishop on f4 but cannot preserve the equal footing that Be7 maintains.

White's best move holds the balance at (+0.13, Stockfish:16) along [pv:f6 gxf6 axb3 Be6 c4], immediately weakening Black's pawn structure with doubled, isolated, and backward pawns that are harder to defend. At the cost of a line that could leave White with doubled b-pawns, it keeps clearer structural pressure than the comparable axb3, which leads to equality via [pv:axb3 Bxf5 Qf3 Qd7 Bg5] with a knight for a bishop and the a-file open for the rook.

per_ply.human_comment:
Perhaps, as a last attempt to stop the imminent
catastrophe, Steinitz could have tried 13...Be6 14.Qh5 Qd7.
per_ply.system_comment: Rather than 13...Be6, a comparable option that leads to equality and may steer White into a weakened pawn structure with doubled pawns that are awkward to handle, 13...d5 concedes a slight advantage to White (+0.03 → +0.53, Stockfish:16) along [pv:d5 Qh5 d4 Bh6 Rg8]. The central break may set Black's pieces and rooks to become more active on the open files, but at the cost of leaving the king under pressure deeper in the line—especially once White continues with Qh5. 13...Be6 leads to equality along [pv:Be6 c4 d5 Qf3 Qd7].

Qh5 is the most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+0.43, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Qh5 d4 Bh6 Rg8 Bf4], steering toward lines where Black may leave a piece hanging and White's pieces could become more actively placed—active pieces coordinate better in attack. If Black later meets it with...Qd6, White's edge only grows. Qf3 is a roughly comparable option that leads to equality along [pv:Qf3 Qd6 Bf4 Qc6 c4], where White may prepare a pawn break on the c-file instead.

per_ply.human_comment:
It is a bit difficult to think that Black could have escaped by sacrificing a
Rook for a minor piece: 14...0-0 15.Bh6. And what if Steinitz wanted to save
this too playing 15...Re8?  Then after 16.Nc3 he could have left the table and
go sell nuts and beans at the Astor movie theather in his hometown.
per_ply.system_comment: 14...Qd6 makes matters worse, and White now has a clear advantage (+0.43 → +1.45, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Qd6 Nc3 Be6 Nb5 Qb8]. Black does put White's king under pressure, keeping the defender focused on king safety, and the line may eventually leave White with a hanging piece. Those gains are outweighed here, and Black missed the more solid 14...d4, which leads to a slight advantage for White [pv:d4 Na3 O-O Bh6 Be6].

The most accurate move maintains White's advantage (+1.32, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nc3 Be6 Nb5 Qd8 Rxe6], steering toward a line where White's king may grow safer and Black's pieces could turn passive, in return for eventually allowing Black to win a pawn in the variation—a trade that may sting once imprecise replies deepen White's grip. c4 leads to a slight advantage for White [pv:c4 d4 Na3 O-O Nb5] by immediately preparing a c-file pawn break, but it is clearly weaker than this active knight jump.

per_ply.system_comment: 16...Qc6 makes matters worse, handing White a decisive advantage (+1.38 → +3.70, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Qc6 Rxe6 Qxe6 Nc7+ Kd7]. White punishes it with Rxe6, and the line may leave White with a queen for a rook and a pawn—a material edge that often decides games. Black missed the potential to win a pawn and leave White's pieces passive with 16...Qb8, which leads to a clear advantage for White along [pv:Qb8 Rxe6 axb5 Rxa8 Qxa8].

The most accurate move maintains White's advantage (+3.68, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Rxe6 Qxe6 Nc7+ Kd7 Nxe6], at the cost of a line that may eventually leave Black with an improved pawn structure. Bf4, which leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:Bf4 O-O Nc7 Kh8 Nxa8], would have placed White's pieces more actively right away and could have won the exchange for a pawn deeper in the variation, but Rxe6 is clearly stronger and keeps White on track to build growing pressure on the king.

18...Kd8 fights back, though White keeps a decisive advantage (+3.17, Stockfish:16), as [pv:Kd8 Qxf7 Qe8 Qg7 Rg8] shows, at the cost of a line that may leave White's king safe. Rg8 was a comparable option—also leaving White with a decisive advantage via [pv:Rg8 Rae1 Qd7 Rxe7+ Qxe7]—that immediately activates the rooks on the open files while a safer king may emerge deeper in that line, but Kd8 holds up slightly better in the fight. White's Qxf7 next will keep the pressure on Black's king building.

The most accurate move maintains White's advantage (+3.34, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Qxf7 Qe8 Qg7 Rf8 Rae1], immediately putting Black's king under pressure—a target that often forces the defender to weaken elsewhere. In return, Black eliminates the doubled pawns. By contrast, c4, which gives White a winning advantage [pv:c4 Qe8 Re2 Qd7 Bf4], prepares a c-file break and may leave Black's back rank vulnerable in the line, but Qxf7 is clearly stronger for its direct kingside pressure.

19...Re8 makes matters worse for Black, and White now has a decisive advantage (+3.34 → +6.16, Stockfish:16). After [pv:Re8 Rae1 Qd7 Bg7 Rc8], White's edge only grows. Black missed the chance to leave a White piece hanging and to target the queen on f7 with 19...Qe8, which still leaves White with a decisive advantage but was materially better: [pv:Qe8 Qg7 Rf8 Rae1 Rf7]. Further along the line, exchanging on f6 may hand White a forcing attack.

per_ply.system_comment: The best move, extending White's advantage (+6.51, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Rae1 Qd7 Bg7 Rc8 Rxe7], may lead to White holding a queen, bishop, and pawn for a rook—a lopsided trade that typically leaves the side with the queen in charge. The line can later turn sharply forcing as White hunts the king. Bf4 leaves White with a decisive advantage too but is clearly weaker: [pv:Bf4 Qd7 Rae1 Rc8 Bd2].

21...Rc8 leaves White with a decisive advantage (+6.14, Stockfish:16). In [pv:Rc8 Rxe7 Rxe7 Bxf6 Kc7], White plays Rxe7, Black recaptures, White exchanges on f6, and...Kc7 does not change the evaluation—and further along White may drive a forcing sequence Black cannot fully meet. Qxe6 was a roughly comparable option that also leaves White with a decisive advantage [pv:Qxe6 Rxe6 Rc8 Rxe7 Rxe7].

Exchanging on f6 hands White a forcing attack—22...Bxf6 leads to forced mate for White (#8 for White, Stockfish:16) [pv:Bxf6 Qxf6+ Kc7 Qe5+ Kd8], as the queen check drives the king forward and the sequence runs out of defenses. Black missed the chance to play 22...Rc7, which still leaves White with a decisive advantage [pv:Rc7 Rxe7 Qxe7 Qxd5+ Kc8] but avoids the immediate mating net.

per_ply.human_comment: The shortest way. Now one could announce mate in seven (Fritz says).
per_ply.system_comment: White's 23.Qxf6+ leads to forced mate for White (#7 for White, Stockfish:16), starting a forcing sequence Black cannot meet: [pv:Qxf6+ Kc7 Qe5+ Kd8 Rxe8+]. In this endgame, a checking queen on f6 is the direct route to conversion—White's job is simply to keep the king tied down until the attack runs its course. After...Kc7, that king step gains Black nothing and only allows White's forcing continuation; deeper in the line White could drive the king to d8 before Rxe8+ settles matters. With so few pieces left, this is an endgame now: king activity and pawns decide it. White remains firmly better going into it.

23...Kc7 leads to forced mate for White. Black gains nothing from the king step and instead allows White's forcing continuation; deeper in the line White could win a queen and a pawn on material, a margin that typically settles endgames of this type. (#7 for White, Stockfish:16) [pv:Kc7 Qe5+ Kd8 Rxe8+ Qxe8] White went on to win the game.
